extracted.intended_audience: Recipients of Federal financial assistance (educational institutions and employers), Title IX coordinators, compliance officers, HR/legal counsel, and policy stakeholders
extracted.subtask_description: Regulatory guidance explaining how recipients must treat pregnancy and pregnancy-related conditions under Title IX for students and employees, including comparisons to other temporary medical conditions, limits on certification requirements, leave and reasonable modification obligations, and related employment protections.

rubrics_metrics.name: §106.40(b)(4) comparability requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Final §106.40(b)(4) states that, to the extent consistent with paragraph (b)(3), a recipient must treat pregnancy or related conditions in the same manner and under the same policies as any other temporary medical condition with respect to any medical or hospital benefit, service, plan, or policy the recipient administers, operates, offers, or participates in with respect to students admitted to the recipient's education program or activity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department revised proposed language to remove references to "disability" and to change "physical condition" to "medical condition" to make clear comparators include psychological or emotional conditions. The defined term "pregnancy or related conditions" includes medical conditions related to pregnancy, childbirth, termination of pregnancy, lactation, or recovery, and thus includes resulting disabilities. This revision is intended to avoid implying pregnancy alone is a disability and to ensure pregnancy-related conditions are compared to other temporary medical conditions (not limited only to purely physical conditions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Application limited 'to the extent consistent with' §106.40(b)(3)
rubrics_metrics.description: §106.40(b)(4) applies only "to the extent consistent with" a recipient's obligations under §106.40(b)(3).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department interprets "consistent with" to mean §106.40(b)(4) applies when doing so would not deny or limit any person's rights or the recipient's obligations under §106.40(b)(3). In other words, §106.40(b)(3) provides a floor beneath which treatment of pregnancy-related conditions may not fall. Recipients must be able to meet §106.40(b)(3) responsibilities (e.g., reasonable modifications, leave, lactation space); when consistent, the comparability requirement of (b)(4) also applies. Example: if (b)(3) requires breaks during class, those must be provided; if the recipient's non-pregnancy temporary medical condition policy is more generous, it must be applied to pregnant students; if less generous, it must not be applied where it would deprive rights under (b)(3).

rubrics_metrics.name: §106.40(b)(3) required actions for students
rubrics_metrics.description: §106.40(b)(3) requires recipients to take specific actions to prevent discrimination and ensure equal access related to pregnancy or related conditions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of specific actions include providing reasonable modifications, leave, and access to lactation space. These obligations form the mandatory floor; recipients cannot use (b)(4) to provide lesser protections than (b)(3). The final rules sometimes permit simpler processes for pregnancy-related needs because pregnancy is time-limited and needs are often foreseeable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on discriminatory recipient policies (even without an individual request)
rubrics_metrics.description: §106.40(b)(4) prohibits recipient policies that treat pregnant students differently from students with other temporary medical conditions, regardless of whether an individual student requests a reasonable modification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: a policy that allows students with temporary medical conditions (including temporary disabilities) free at-home tutoring but states that option is not available to pregnant students would violate §106.40(b)(4). The prohibition applies even if no single pregnant student has requested the tutoring.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on requiring certification of physical ability except narrow circumstances (§106.40(b)(5))
rubrics_metrics.description: Final §106.40(b)(5) states a recipient may not require a pregnant student to certify physical ability before participation unless the certification satisfies §106.40(b)(5)(i)-(iii).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The rule expands the prohibition to certifications by non-healthcare providers or "any other person." The three conditions under which a certification may be required are: (i) the certified level of physical ability or health is necessary for participation in the class, program, or extracurricular activity (e.g., walking at a fast pace for 20 minutes), (ii) the recipient requires such certification of all students participating in the class, program, or activity, and (iii) the information obtained is not used as a basis for discrimination prohibited by Title IX. The Department removed the prior regulation's reference to emotional ability to avoid stereotyping; emotional ability certifications remain subject to general prohibitions on sex discrimination and may implicate disability law if applicable. The provision balances preventing burdensome/documentary requirements driven by stereotypes with recipient safety interests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comparator for certification and exclusion decisions
rubrics_metrics.description: When determining whether a pregnant student is being subject to different treatment (e.g., certification or exclusion), recipients should compare the pregnant student to the general student population, not be limited to students receiving medical attention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department explains that comparison to the general student population is usually appropriate because most pregnant students have no limitation relevant to participation. The rule rejects the suggestion that comparators must be limited (citing Young v. United Parcel Service, Inc.) and clarifies that other comparators may also be acceptable; the goal is to ensure pregnant students are not treated differently due to pregnancy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Voluntary leave for pregnancy must be granted consistent with medical necessity
rubrics_metrics.description: Title IX has long required that voluntary leave for pregnancy or related conditions be granted consistent with medical necessity; final §106.40(b)(3)(iv) requires recipients to permit voluntary leave for pregnancy or related conditions without requiring additional steps that might be imposed for non-pregnancy temporary medical conditions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department acknowledges that processes for obtaining leave may differ for non-pregnancy temporary medical conditions, but those additional steps cannot be required of pregnant students seeking voluntary leave. This protects against burdensome procedural hurdles that would effectively disadvantage pregnant students.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pregnancy is not a disability per se; disability law may also apply
rubrics_metrics.description: The Department reemphasizes that pregnancy, standing alone, is not a disability, although some pregnancy-related conditions or complications might qualify as disabilities under Section 504 or the ADA; if so, those laws may apply alongside Title IX.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The rule clarifies that §106.40(b)(4) requires comparable treatment to temporary medical conditions regardless of whether the pregnancy-related condition meets the legal definition of a disability. Where a pregnancy-related condition does qualify as a disability and a recipient's disability policy is more generous, those disability accommodations must be provided.

rubrics_metrics.name: §106.57 employment protections for pregnancy or related conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: Final §106.57 prohibits discrimination against employees based on current, potential, or past pregnancy or related conditions and requires that recipients treat an employee's pregnancy or related conditions as they do any other temporary medical conditions for all job-related purposes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The examples of job-related purposes include commencement, duration and extensions of leave, payment of disability income, accrual of seniority, reinstatement, and any other benefit or service and under any fringe benefit offered by virtue of employment. The Department declined to require reasonable modifications for employees at this time, citing interplay with recent federal legislation (e.g., PUMP Act, PWFA) and pending rulemaking, but notes that §106.57(c) itself is broad and intended to effectuate Title IX's nondiscrimination mandate for employees.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parental, family, or marital status protections for employees (§106.57(a))
rubrics_metrics.description: §106.57(a) prohibits sex discrimination against employees on the basis of parental, family, or marital status.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department retained these longstanding protections and made minor wording edits (replacing "apply" with "implement", "shall" with "must", and "Which" with "That") for clarity. The Department declined to require reasonable modifications for parenting employees at this time, while noting the prohibition on different treatment based on sex still applies and that recipients are prohibited from discriminating based on sex stereotypes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Independent contractor coverage is not mandated but may be voluntary
rubrics_metrics.description: The Department declined to mandate that §106.57 cover independent contractors; to the extent a contractor is an employee of the recipient, the contractor is entitled to protections; a recipient may choose to cover independent contractors voluntarily.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationale includes need for more information about cost, administrative burden, interplay with common law principles and other legal requirements, and variations in state employment law. The Department notes nothing in the final regulations prohibits a recipient from choosing to cover independent contractors under §106.57.

rubrics_metrics.name: 'Medical or hospital' modifier retained and scope clarified
rubrics_metrics.description: The Department declined to remove the words "medical or hospital" that modify "benefit, service, plan, or policy" in §106.40(b)(4) and explained the provision's historical language dating to 1975.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although the modifier remains, the Department explains that the reasonable modifications framework in §106.40(b)(3) alleviates potential ambiguity about the scope of protections. The final text also clarifies that §106.40(b)(4) applies only when consistent with the recipient's (b)(3) obligations.
